stories.title: Binance says fake job interviews opened the door to its $6.3bn heist
points: Binance's own investigation says the thieves behind last week's theft, which the FBI blames on the North Korea-linked group TraderTraitor, posed as recruiters and gave an engineer an interview task laced with malware.
That foothold, plus an earlier tampered download on another engineer's laptop, let them use Binance's in-house AI tool to take over colleagues' machines and trigger the attack on 29 October.
The exchange says it has rebuilt its wallet systems and AI tools, set aside money to cover users' losses and reopened withdrawals.
numbers: stolen in the biggest heist on record
stories.why: The weakest point in a crypto vault was a job seeker's trust. As companies wire AI agents into their systems, one infected laptop can now reach much further than it used to.
stories.other: This is Binance describing its own breach, and it is keeping some security details private. Its account may stress the attackers' cunning over its own control gaps; an independent review would tell more.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: how fake job interviews led to the $6.3bn Binance heist
stories.emailTeaser: How a fake recruiter opened the door to a record crypto theft

stories.title: AI's borrowing bill is rising as bond buyers demand more
points: The FT's editorial board notes that Alphabet, Meta and Oracle went back to bond markets this week but had to pay clearly more than a few months ago; Oracle's new bonds carry coupons above 8.5%.
Insuring against default is dearer too: protection on Meta's debt now costs about 1.2% a year, which the board likens to junk-rated South Africa.
Its view: the AI boom may not end with a stock crash but with a slow squeeze in credit. Oracle has even pledged to cap the new money it raises from markets until 2030.
numbers: yearly cost to insure Meta's debt
stories.why: Dearer money raises the return every data centre has to earn. If cash-rich, top-rated giants pay more, smaller AI borrowers and the lenders behind them face a much harder test.
stories.other: These firms still hold strong ratings and cash-rich core businesses, and they are still raising huge sums. Repricing risk is credit markets working, not breaking.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: rising borrowing costs for AI giants
stories.emailTeaser: Bond buyers want more to fund the data centre boom

stories.title: Europe's supermarket freezer hacks: what we know so far
points: On Monday hackers remotely pushed freezer temperatures as high as 55C in almost 100 stores across Sweden, Finland, Ireland, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia, weeks after a similar overnight wave hit French supermarkets.

The trick was simple: known flaws in internet-linked temperature controllers. Danfoss and Copeland confirmed affected systems; shops kept off the public internet or behind private networks were spared.
No one has claimed it. A Sentinel researcher suspects a Russia-linked group seeking deniable disruption, and EU officials call it an attack on food security.
numbers: peak freezer temperature set by hackers
stories.why: Cheap hacks with costly results are the new frontier. Freezers, pumps and boilers now sit online, and many owners lack the budget or skills to lock them down.
stories.other: Blame rests on one researcher's reading of thin traces, and the fix is routine patching. Calling it state warfare could overstate what copycats might also pull off.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: how hackers turned up supermarket freezers
stories.emailTeaser: Hackers thaw supermarket freezers and nobody owns up

stories.title: AI is shutting the door on new hires, not pushing workers out
points: Sarah O'Connor argues the real AI jobs shock is fewer hires, not mass lay-offs. History fits: boot-sewing machines in Victorian England choked off new artisans rather than sacking existing ones.

Today's signs match. Lay-offs stay low, entry-level software hiring is falling while demand for seniors holds, Danish firms using AI simply hire more slowly, and call centres shrink because hiring slowed.
She wants policy aimed at the young: closer ties between schools and employers and more support for start-ups, since retraining schemes such as Sweden's often leave them out.
stories.why: Lay-off numbers can look calm while a generation struggles to land its first job. For countries with big young workforces, India among them, slower entry hiring matters more than headline cuts.
stories.other: It is early and the data are thin. A recession could still bring abrupt cuts, and young people have often adapted fastest to new technology.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: AI shrinks hiring rather than causing lay-offs
stories.emailHead: AI's jobs hit: fewer first jobs
stories.emailTeaser: The damage shows up at the door, not the exit

stories.title: The new Fragile Five are rich nations, a Mint column argues
points: Narayan Ramachandran takes the 2013 label once pinned on Turkey, Brazil, India, South Africa and Indonesia and hands it to France, Italy, the UK, Germany and the US: fragile now in social, not currency, terms.

Higher rates swell debt costs while inflation and an oil shock squeeze budgets. France's student protests have grown into a cost-of-living revolt against a fiscal deficit above 5% of GDP, and Italy has seen looting and fuel blockades.
He rates Germany the least at risk of the five.
numbers: France's fiscal deficit, share of GDP
stories.why: India was on the old list and now watches the roles reverse. Unrest in big rich economies can dent demand for Indian exports and keep oil and interest rates jumpy.
stories.other: Floating reserve currencies and deep bond markets give these nations room the old Fragile Five never had. Street protests are not defaults, and the label may stretch the comparison.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: why rich G7 nations look fragile
stories.emailTeaser: France, Italy, UK, Germany and US look shaky now

stories.title: Is 'Made in China' heading for its 'Made in Japan' moment?
points: Bloomberg Opinion's Howard Chua-Eoan, in Mint, recalls when 'Made in Japan' was a joke for flimsy toys, until firms like Nippon Kogaku (now Nikon) and Totsuko (now Sony) made it a badge of quality.
He sees China at a similar turn: Shenzhen lens maker Viltrox is joining the elite, and Europeans buy Chinese EVs that an HSBC report judged simply better.
Yet many Chinese brands play down their roots, from Miniso's Uniqlo-like logo to Temu's offshore legal home. He expects that to fade as confidence grows.
stories.why: If Chinese brands start selling their origin as a plus, rivals from Europe to India lose the easy line that cheaper means worse.
stories.other: Japan rose in an era of open markets; China faces tariffs, quotas and security worries. Keeping a low profile may be smart strategy, not shyness.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: from Made in Japan to Made in China
stories.emailTeaser: Why Chinese brands may stop hiding where they're from

stories.title: Bank Hapoalim says free shares made new investors, backing Musk
points: In the WSJ, Bank Hapoalim's spokesperson praises Elon Musk's plan to give one SpaceX share to every American child next year.

Israel's largest retail bank offered customers two of its shares or a cash grant in 2025. In the first round, about 240,000 people who had never held securities with it became shareholders, and it added a free investing-basics platform.
Her case: owning even one share makes people curious about prices, dividends and earnings, and the first step is the hardest.
stories.why: Gifting shares is a cheap way to widen market participation, a live question wherever household savings sit mostly in cash, gold or deposits.
stories.other: The author speaks for the bank that ran the scheme, and a gift share doubles as marketing. Musk's plan is still a promise, and real financial literacy takes more than one stock.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: what gifting single shares does for new investors
stories.emailHead: One free share, a new investor
stories.emailTeaser: An Israeli bank's case for Musk's SpaceX gift

takeaway.line: Today's risks slip in through side doors: a job test, a freezer dial, a bond coupon, an unfilled first job. Watch the quiet entrances, not just the front gate.

coverAlt: Fake hires, hot freezers, dear bonds, shaky G7, proud China. Kids get stock. Grads don't.
